claim: The inferior olive provides the climbing fibers to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex.
source: The inferior olive provides the climbing fibers to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex, where they elicit all-or-none complex spikes and control major forms of plasticity.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact supported by citation to Ito, 1984 in the introduction.

claim: Climbing fibers elicit all-or-none complex spikes in Purkinje cells.
source: The inferior olive provides the climbing fibers to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex, where they elicit all-or-none complex spikes and control major forms of plasticity.
evidence: This is a well-established physiological property supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Climbing fibers control major forms of plasticity in the cerebellar cortex.
source: The inferior olive provides the climbing fibers to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex, where they elicit all-or-none complex spikes and control major forms of plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction regarding plasticity mechanisms.

claim: When excitatory input is activated approximately 50 ms after inhibitory input, the phase of intrinsic oscillations becomes unstable and excitatory input can hardly generate any olivary spike.
source: When the excitatory input is activated shortly (~50 ms) after the inhibitory input, the phase of the intrinsic oscillations becomes remarkably unstable and the excitatory input can hardly generate any olivary spike.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6, demonstrating minimal spike probability at this interval.

claim: When excitatory input is activated approximately 150 ms after inhibitory input, excitatory input can optimally drive olivary spiking.
source: Instead, when the excitatory input is activated one cycle (~150 ms) after the inhibitory input, the excitatory input can optimally drive olivary spiking, riding on top of the first cycle of the subthreshold oscillations that have been powerfully reset by the preceding inhibitory input.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6, demonstrating maximal spike probability at this interval.

claim: Inhibitory input powerfully resets subthreshold oscillations in olivary neurons.
source: Instead, when the excitatory input is activated one cycle (~150 ms) after the inhibitory input, the excitatory input can optimally drive olivary spiking, riding on top of the first cycle of the subthreshold oscillations that have been powerfully reset by the preceding inhibitory input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing strong phase resetting following CN stimulation.

claim: The inferior olive forms an integral part of the cerebellar system.
source: The inferior olive (IO) forms an integral part of the cerebellar system in that it provides all the climbing fibers innervating Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex (Ito, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ito, 1984 and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Activation of climbing fiber terminals evokes both short-term and long-term effects.
source: Activation of the climbing fiber terminals elicits both short-term and long-term effects (De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Zeeuw et al., 2011.

claim: Complex spikes are powerful, all-or-none depolarizations in Purkinje cells.
source: In the short-term, it evokes powerful, all-or-none, depolarizations in Purkinje cells also known as complex spikes (Thach, 1967)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thach, 1967 and represents established physiological knowledge.

claim: Increases in complex spike activity within cerebellar microzones can facilitate reflex-like movements.
source: increases in complex spike activity within cerebellar microzones can facilitate reflex-like movements, such as fast reactive limb movements following a perturbation (De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Gruijl et al., 2014a and Hoogland et al., 2015.

claim: Widespread ensembles of complex spike activity mediate more demanding forms of motor behavior.
source: but when occurring in more widespread ensembles they also mediate more demanding forms of motor behavior, such as skilled sequences of contractions of tongue muscles upon presentation of specific sensory cues (Welsh et al., 1995; Bina et al., 2022; Romano et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Welsh et al., 1995; Bina et al., 2022; and Romano et al., 2022.

claim: Modulation of climbing fiber activity facilitates the induction of various forms of pre- and postsynaptic plasticity at parallel fiber synapses.
source: In the more long term, modulation of climbing fiber activity facilitates the induction of various forms of pre- and postsynaptic plasticity at most, if not all, parallel fiber synapses onto interneurons and Purkinje cells in the molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2012.

claim: Climbing fibers are prominently implicated in cerebellar learning.
source: Due to the fact that these different subcellular effects occur in a synergistic fashion in that they ultimately converge into either a downbound or upbound impact on simple spike activity in the Purkinje cells (De Zeeuw, 2021), climbing fibers are also prominently implicated in cerebellar learning (Ito and Kano, 1982; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Safo and Regehr, 2008; ten Brinke et al., 2015 and ten Brinke et al., 2019; Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017; Boele et al., 2018; Bina et al., 2022; Romano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Ito and Kano, 1982; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; and others.

claim: Enhanced synchronization of complex spikes within microzones shortens the latency of subsequent reflex movements.
source: For example, when the synchronization of complex spikes within microzones is enhanced, the latency of subsequent reflex movements will be shortened (Kistler et al., 2002; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; De Gruijl et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kistler et al., 2002; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; and De Gruijl et al., 2014a.

claim: The timing of climbing fiber activity with respect to parallel fiber activity determines whether depression or potentiation plasticity mechanisms prevail in Purkinje cells.
source: Or likewise, depending on the timing of the activity of the climbing fiber input with respect to that of the parallel fiber input, depression or potentiation plasticity mechanisms in Purkinje cells will prevail (Wang et al., 2000; De Zeeuw, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000 and De Zeeuw, 2021.

claim: Olivary neurons are endowed with dendro-dendritic gap junctions.
source: Classical work by Llinas and Yarom has revealed that olivary neurons are endowed with dendro-dendritic gap junctions as well as ionic conductances that allow them to oscillate in synchrony (Llinas et al., 1974; Sotelo et al., 1974; Llinás and Yarom, 1981; Llinás and Yarom, 1986; Lampl and Yarom, 1993; Lampl and Yarom, 1997; Leznik and Llinás, 2005; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Llinas et al., 1974 and Sotelo et al., 1974.

claim: Olivary neurons possess ionic conductances that allow them to oscillate in synchrony.
source: Classical work by Llinas and Yarom has revealed that olivary neurons are endowed with dendro-dendritic gap junctions as well as ionic conductances that allow them to oscillate in synchrony (Llinas et al., 1974; Sotelo et al., 1974; Llinás and Yarom, 1981; Llinás and Yarom, 1986; Lampl and Yarom, 1993; Lampl and Yarom, 1997; Leznik and Llinás, 2005; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Llinás and Yarom, 1981 and 1986.

claim: Olivary neurons can show different types of subthreshold activity.
source: More specifically, olivary neurons can show different types of subthreshold activity (Khosrovani et al., 2007; Turecek et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Khosrovani et al., 2007 and Turecek et al., 2014.

claim: Differential expression of Cav 3.1 channels (T-type Ca+2) can partly explain different types of subthreshold activity in olivary neurons.
source: which can partly be explained at the cellular level by differential expression of Cav 3.1 channels (T-type Ca+2) (Urbano et al., 2006; Bazzigaluppi and de Jeu, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Urbano et al., 2006 and Bazzigaluppi and de Jeu, 2016.

claim: Olivary subthreshold oscillations are likely to occur at preferred frequencies below 10 Hz for a limited number of cycles.
source: Whole-cell recordings in vivo, systems' extracellular recordings, as well as modeling studies indicate that olivary subthreshold oscillations (STOs) are likely to occur at preferred frequencies below 10 Hz for a limited number of cycles and that the complex spikes ride on this rhythm (Sasaki et al., 1989; Bal and McCormick, 1997; Blenkinsop and Lang, 2006; Chorev et al., 2007; Choi et al., 2010; Lefler et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2016; Lang et al., 2017; Khosrovani et al., 2007; Negrello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Sasaki et al., 1989; Bal and McCormick, 1997; and others.

claim: Complex spikes ride on the rhythm of subthreshold oscillations.
source: Whole-cell recordings in vivo, systems' extracellular recordings, as well as modeling studies indicate that olivary subthreshold oscillations (STOs) are likely to occur at preferred frequencies below 10 Hz for a limited number of cycles and that the complex spikes ride on this rhythm (Sasaki et al., 1989; Bal and McCormick, 1997; Blenkinsop and Lang, 2006; Chorev et al., 2007; Choi et al., 2010; Lefler et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2016; Lang et al., 2017; Khosrovani et al., 2007; Negrello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Negrello et al., 2019.

claim: The vast majority of axon terminals of olivary afferents target dendritic spines located in the olivary glomeruli.
source: The vast majority of the axon terminals of the afferents target the dendritic spines located in the olivary glomeruli (Sotelo et al., 1974; de Zeeuw et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sotelo et al., 1974 and de Zeeuw et al., 1989.

claim: Many dendritic spines in olivary glomeruli are electronically coupled by gap junctions.
source: Many of these spines are electronically coupled by gap junctions and most, if not all, of them receive both an inhibitory and excitatory input (de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Zeeuw et al., 1989 and De Zeeuw et al., 1990.

claim: Most, if not all, dendritic spines in olivary glomeruli receive both an inhibitory and excitatory input.
source: Many of these spines are electronically coupled by gap junctions and most, if not all, of them receive both an inhibitory and excitatory input (de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Zeeuw et al., 1989 and De Zeeuw et al., 1990.

claim: Spike generation of olivary neurons may be highly sensitive to the temporal interval between activation of inhibitory and excitatory inputs.
source: Based upon a theoretical model of excitable spines in such configuration (Segev and Parnas, 1983; Segev and Rall, 1988), it has been advocated that spike generation of olivary neurons may be highly sensitive to the temporal interval between activation of the inhibitory and excitatory inputs (De Zeeuw, 1990; De Zeeuw et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models (Segev and Parnas, 1983; Segev and Rall, 1988) and De Zeeuw, 1990; De Zeeuw et al., 1998.

claim: The principal olive and rostral medial accessory olive receive monosynaptic inhibitory inputs from the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of olivary neurons in combination with dual color optogenetics, we set out to test this hypothesis in mice by investigating the temporal response properties of neurons in the principal olive (PO) and rostral medial accessory olive (MAO), both of which receive their monosynaptic, inhibitory and excitatory inputs from the cerebellar nuclei (CN) and mesodiencephalic junction (MDJ), respectively (de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; Ruigrok and Voogd, 1990; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Lefler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; Ruigrok and Voogd, 1990; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; and Lefler et al., 2014.

claim: The principal olive and rostral medial accessory olive receive monosynaptic excitatory inputs from the mesodiencephalic junction.
source: Using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of olivary neurons in combination with dual color optogenetics, we set out to test this hypothesis in mice by investigating the temporal response properties of neurons in the principal olive (PO) and rostral medial accessory olive (MAO), both of which receive their monosynaptic, inhibitory and excitatory inputs from the cerebellar nuclei (CN) and mesodiencephalic junction (MDJ), respectively (de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; Ruigrok and Voogd, 1990; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Lefler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; Ruigrok and Voogd, 1990; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; and Lefler et al., 2014.

claim: Optimal and stable control of olivary spiking behavior strongly depends on the temporal interval between cerebellar inhibition and mesodiencephalic excitation.
source: Our data indicate that optimal and stable control of olivary spiking behavior indeed strongly depends on the temporal interval between cerebellar inhibition and mesodiencephalic excitation, allowing bidirectional control of firing probability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Stimulation of excitatory input at the appropriate moment following inhibition triggers more olivary spikes than stimulation of excitatory input alone.
source: The sensitivity to this interval is so high that stimulation of the excitatory input at the appropriate moment following inhibition triggers more olivary spikes than stimulation of the excitatory input alone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C comparing spike probabilities.

claim: Inhibition induces a strong phase reset of subthreshold oscillations.
source: The in vitro experiments confirmed by simulations running on a realistic model of the mouse IO indicate that this high sensitivity results at least in part from the fact that inhibition induces a strong phase reset of the STOs on top of which the excitatory input can drive the spiking output.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and modeling data in Figure 4.

claim: The size of the olivary network engaged in generating a particular firing pattern depends on the timing and overlap between inhibitory and excitatory inputs.
source: Moreover, the simulations of coupled olivary neurons also suggest that the size of the olivary network that is engaged in generating a particular firing pattern also depends on the timing and overlap between both inputs.
evidence: This is supported by modeling data shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: An average of 5.1±6.9 dye-coupled neurons per patched cell was obtained in slices of 300 μm thickness.
source: Using this approach in slices of 300 μm thickness, we obtained an average of 5.1±6.9 dye-coupled neurons per patched cell (range: 0–27; n=20, N=17), which is in line with previous in vitro studies (De Zeeuw et al., 2003; Placantonakis et al., 2006; Turecek et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from biocytin labeling experiments.

claim: 69% of IO neurons displayed subthreshold oscillations during spontaneous activity.
source: Across all recordings 69% of the IO neurons (69/100 cells; N=43) displayed STOs during spontaneous activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Oscillating and non-oscillating IO cells did not differ in their passive membrane properties.
source: The oscillating and non-oscillating cell groups did not differ in their passive membrane properties (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E with statistical analysis.

claim: The membrane potential of oscillating cells averaged –54.52±5.69 mV.
source: Neither the membrane potential (oscillating cells: an average of –54.52±5.69 mV ranging from –67.29 to –40.24 mV; non-oscillating cells: an average of 53.62±7.14 mV ranging from –66.86 to –39.8 mV)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: The input resistance of oscillating cells averaged 44.49±17.83 MΩ.
source: nor the input resistance (oscillating cells: an average of 44.49±17.83 MΩ ranging from 13.82 to 87.09 MΩ; non-oscillating cells: an average of 47.64±16.64 MΩ ranging from 20.2 to 97.46 MΩ) differed significantly among the two cell types (p=0.49 and p=0.40, respectively; unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Oscillations of cells with STOs had a mean amplitude of 9.52±5.4 mV.
source: Oscillations of cells with STOs had a mean amplitude of 9.52±5.4 mV (range: 1.13–21.14 mV) and a mean frequency of 4.97±1.85 Hz (ranging from 1.63 to 9.77 Hz) (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Oscillations of cells with STOs had a mean frequency of 4.97±1.85 Hz.
source: Oscillations of cells with STOs had a mean amplitude of 9.52±5.4 mV (range: 1.13–21.14 mV) and a mean frequency of 4.97±1.85 Hz (ranging from 1.63 to 9.77 Hz) (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: IO responses to activation of inhibitory synapses from the CN consist of a GABAAR-mediated hyperpolarization followed by a rebound depolarization.
source: IO responses to activation of the inhibitory synapses from the CN consist of a GABAAR-mediated hyperpolarization (Vhyp) followed by a rebound depolarization (Vreb), reliant on low voltage-gated T-type calcium channels and HCN channels (Choi et al., 2010; Bal and McCormick, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2010 and Bal and McCormick, 1997, and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The rebound depolarization following CN stimulation is reliant on low voltage-gated T-type calcium channels and HCN channels.
source: IO responses to activation of the inhibitory synapses from the CN consist of a GABAAR-mediated hyperpolarization (Vhyp) followed by a rebound depolarization (Vreb), reliant on low voltage-gated T-type calcium channels and HCN channels (Choi et al., 2010; Bal and McCormick, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2010 and Bal and McCormick, 1997.

claim: Application of picrotoxin completely blocked Vhyp and Vreb following CN stimulation.
source: Application of the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin completely blocked Vhyp and Vreb (n=5 and N=4; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), underscoring the GABAergic nature of the response.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of CN afferents induced transient oscillations in 38.2% of non-oscillating cells.
source: Optogenetic stimulation (20 ms light pulses, 0.4–3.85 mW/mm2) of CN afferents in the IO in vitro induced transient oscillations in 38.2% of non-oscillating cells (12 out of 31 cells; N=25), which is in line with previous data obtained in vivo (Khosrovani et al., 2007; Bazzigaluppi and de Jeu, 2016).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data supported by citations to Khosrovani et al., 2007 and Bazzigaluppi and de Jeu, 2016.

claim: CN-induced transient oscillations lasted up to 2.88 s with an average duration of 1.8±0.65 s.
source: Such oscillations, which lasted up to 2.88 s (average duration of 1.8±0.65 s; n=5, N=4), could only be induced if the hyperpolarizing component of the synaptic potential (Vhyp) had a magnitude of at least 1.14 mV (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CN-induced transient oscillations could only be induced if Vhyp had a magnitude of at least 1.14 mV.
source: Such oscillations, which lasted up to 2.88 s (average duration of 1.8±0.65 s; n=5, N=4), could only be induced if the hyperpolarizing component of the synaptic potential (Vhyp) had a magnitude of at least 1.14 mV (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The amplitude of the first cycle following CN stimulation scaled well with the amplitude of Vhyp (r2=0.95).
source: On average, the amplitude of the first cycle following stimulation (Figure 2D, lower panel) scaled well with the amplitude of Vhyp (r2=0.95; n=5, N=4) (Figure 2E, first panel) and was modulated by membrane voltage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2E with correlation analysis.

claim: CN afferent stimulation acted as a strongly resetting stimulus for oscillating IO neurons with a slope of –0.52 ± 0.01.
source: In the subthreshold regime, CN afferent stimulation acted as a strongly resetting stimulus for oscillating IO neurons and consistently introduced a phase delay for each phase of the cycle (slope = –0.52 ± 0.01, ΔФ-intercept = 0.07 ± 0.01, r2=0.86; n=5, N=3) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2G with phase response curve analysis.

claim: Intertrial phase jitter was significantly reduced after CN stimulation.
source: Across trials, intertrial phase jitter was significantly reduced after stimulation (SDpre-stim=59.51 ms, SDpost-stim=20.35 ms, n=15, N=14; p<0.0001, F test), indicating that the stimulus induced nearly identical post-stimulus phase responses across trials (Figure 2F and H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2H with statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic responses could significantly boost STO amplitude for four post-stimulus cycles.
source: Inhibitory synaptic responses could significantly boost STO amplitude (ΔSTO amplitude of first cycle 4.8±3.7 mV, p<0.0001; second cycle 1.0±1.7 mV, p<0.0001; third cycle 0.57±1.7 mV, p<0.0001; fourth cycle 0.4±1.3 mV, n=24, N=19; p=0.0002, Friedman test) (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2I with statistical analysis.

claim: Olivary synaptic responses to excitatory input from the MDJ are comprised of a depolarization mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors.
source: Olivary synaptic responses to excitatory input from the MDJ are comprised of a depolarization (Vdep) mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors (Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014), followed by a hyperpolarization (Vhyp), mediated by both HCN and SK channels (Garden et al., 2017; Garden et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014; Garden et al., 2017; and Garden et al., 2018.

claim: The hyperpolarization following MDJ excitation is mediated by both HCN and SK channels.
source: Olivary synaptic responses to excitatory input from the MDJ are comprised of a depolarization (Vdep) mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors (Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014), followed by a hyperpolarization (Vhyp), mediated by both HCN and SK channels (Garden et al., 2017; Garden et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garden et al., 2017 and Garden et al., 2018.

claim: MDJ stimulation could only trigger STOs in intrinsically silent IO neurons when Vhyp was larger than ~3 mV.
source: In general, stimulation of MDJ afferents could only trigger STOs in intrinsically silent IO neurons when Vhyp was larger than ~3 mV.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from the study.

claim: The duration of MDJ-induced transient oscillations (1.3±0.64 s) was significantly shorter than those occurring upon CN stimulation.
source: The duration of these transient oscillations (1.3±0.64 s, ranging from 0.44 s to 2.36 s) was on average significantly shorter (p=0.005, unpaired t-test; n=6, N=5) than those occurring upon stimulation of the CN afferents.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data with statistical comparison.

claim: MDJ stimulation induced a weak phase resetting in oscillating IO cells.
source: Similarly, in oscillating IO cells, MDJ stimulation induced a weak phase resetting (Figure 3G) and significantly reduced the phase jitter (SDpost-stim=44.97 ms versus SDpre-stim=56.47 ms; p<0.0001, F test; n=16, N=14), but this latter reduction was significantly smaller (p<0.0001, F test) than that following CN stimulation (compare Figure 3F–H with Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: MDJ stimulation induced a relatively weak, yet significant, increase of the amplitude of post-stimulus oscillation cycles.
source: Moreover, MDJ stimulation induced a relatively weak, yet significant, increase of the amplitude of the post-stimulus oscillation cycles in these cells (ΔSTO amplitude of first cycle 1.52±3.0 mV, p<0.0001; second cycle 0.60±2.0 mV, p<0.0001; third cycle 0.37±1.7 mV, p=0.01; fourth cycle 0.5±3.69 mV, p=0.0119; Friedman test, n=26, N=19), (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3I with statistical analysis.

claim: Vhyp and Vreb were not significantly affected by picrotoxin following MDJ stimulation.
source: Vhyp and Vreb were not significantly affected by the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (amplitude change relative to baseline, Vhyp: 138.1 ± 66.6%, p=0.1493; Vreb: 103.7 ± 36.5%, p=0.7852; n=8, N=8, paired t-test), whereas Vdep slightly increased (122.7 ± 13.92 %, p=0.0024) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F with statistical analysis.

claim: CNQX prominently reduced all three components of the MDJ response.
source: Instead, when AMPA receptors were blocked with CNQX all three components were prominently reduced (Vdep: 22.9 ± 12.18%, p<0.0001; Vhyp: 21.2 ± 19.7%, p<0.0001; Vreb: 10.8 ± 12.6%, p<0.0001; n=8, N=8, paired t-test).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: APV caused a further reduction of all three components of the MDJ response after CNQX application.
source: Moreover, application of the NMDA receptor antagonist APV (50 μM) caused a further reduction (Vdep: 7.0 ± 9.7%, p=0.001; Vhyp: 13.8 ± 17.4%, p=0.0022; Vreb: 7.2±14.4, p=0.001; n=4, N=4, paired t-test) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F with statistical analysis.

claim: The IO model comprises over a thousand cells with inhibitory and excitatory arborizations from the CN and MDJ.
source: In this work we have extended the IO model from Negrello et al., 2019, by scaling the number of cells to capture the murine MAO, comprising over a thousand cells with inhibitory and excitatory arborizations from the CN and MDJ, respectively (Vrieler et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study, supported by citation to Vrieler et al., 2019.

claim: The network model can reproduce the strong phase resetting following CN stimulation observed experimentally.
source: Indeed, both the strong phase resetting following CN stimulation (Figure 4A) and the relatively high variability in phase values following MDJ stimulation (Figure 4B) emerge from the model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The network model can reproduce the relatively high variability in phase values following MDJ stimulation observed experimentally.
source: Indeed, both the strong phase resetting following CN stimulation (Figure 4A) and the relatively high variability in phase values following MDJ stimulation (Figure 4B) emerge from the model.
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The PRC slope did not differ significantly across most intervals tested, except for the condition where excitation followed inhibition by 150 ms.
source: The PRC slope reflecting phase changes in relation to the phase of the STO during which stimulation occurred did not differ significantly across any of the intervals tested (Figure 5C and D), except for the condition where excitation followed inhibition by 150 ms (Figure 5E and F); for this interval the slope was significantly steeper (–0.69±0.05; p<0.0001, n=7, N=7, one-way ANOVA) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: The ΔФ-intercept shifted significantly from a negative value at an interval of –100 ms to a positive value at an interval of 150 ms.
source: Moreover, the ΔФ-intercept shifted significantly (p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA) from a negative value at an interval of –100 ms (i.e., excitation preceding inhibition; –0.16±0.02; n=6, N=4) to a positive value at an interval of 150 ms (0.35±0.03; n=7, N=7) (Figure 5C–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: An interval of +150 ms yielded the highest STO amplitude of 7.25±3.45 mV during the first cycle.
source: Indeed, whereas an interval of +150 ms yielded the highest STO amplitude of 7.25±3.45 mV during the first cycle (n=10, N=8), an interval of +50 ms resulted in an amplitude of only 1.83±3.42 mV (n=34, N=25) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: An interval of +50 ms resulted in an STO amplitude of only 1.83±3.42 mV.
source: Indeed, whereas an interval of +150 ms yielded the highest STO amplitude of 7.25±3.45 mV during the first cycle (n=10, N=8), an interval of +50 ms resulted in an amplitude of only 1.83±3.42 mV (n=34, N=25) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the slice preparation, 57% of IO cells analyzed showed spontaneous spikes at a frequency of 0.1±0.1 Hz.
source: Yet, in our slice preparation of the IO 57% of the cells analyzed (32 out of 56 neurons, N=36) showed spontaneous spikes at a significantly lower frequency of 0.1±0.1 Hz (ranging from 0.0017 to 0.34 Hz, membrane voltage range: from –56 to –41 mV).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from the study.

claim: In awake animals the spontaneous firing rate of complex spikes is approximately 1 Hz.
source: In awake animals the spontaneous firing rate of complex spikes is approximately 1 Hz (Ju et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ju et al., 2019.

claim: Spike probability was low when excitation followed inhibition at intervals in the range of 50–70 ms.
source: As expected, spike probability was low when excitation followed inhibition at intervals in the range of 50–70 ms (Pspike = 0 ± 0 in both cases; for 50 ms, n=9, N=8; for 70 ms, n=6, N=6), both near the trough of the hyperpolarizing component of the inhibitory response (Figures 5F and 6C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 6C.

claim: Spike probability was largest at an interval of 150 ms (0.57±0.3).
source: Spike probability was largest at an interval of 150 ms around the peak of the rebound component of the inhibitory response (0.57±0.3; n=9, N=8) (Figures 5F and 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I and J), which coincides with the major resonant frequency of IO cells (Khosrovani et al., 2007; Negrello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 6C with citations to Khosrovani et al., 2007 and Negrello et al., 2019.

claim: The spike probability for the 150 ms interval was significantly higher than for either single inhibitory or excitatory responses.
source: The spike probability for the 150 ms interval was significantly higher than for either single inhibitory (0.01±0.03, n=7, N=6; Figure 6A) or excitatory (0.22±0.28, n=7, N=6; Figure 6B) responses under the same Vm and stimulation strength (150 ms interval with respect to single inhibitory and single excitatory responses p<0.0001 and p=0.0018, respectively; one-way ANOVA) (Figures 5F and 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement1I and J).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: When focal stimulation of the excitatory input to a group of cells occurred one cycle after inhibition onset, the network produced the highest amplitude of rebound, largest spiking probability and effective phase resets.
source: When focal stimulation of the excitatory input to a group of cells occurred one cycle after inhibition onset (cycle T=120 ms, 8 Hz), the network produced the highest amplitude of rebound, largest spiking probability and effective phase resets (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Combined stimulation detached the oscillation of the stimulated group for over a second for most stimulus intervals.
source: For most stimulus intervals, combined stimulation detached the oscillation of the stimulated group, which could last for over a second (Figure 8C and D, Figure 8—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The olivary neuropil is characterized by glomeruli comprising a core of dendritic spines coupled by dendrodendritic gap junctions and surrounded by axon terminals.
source: The olivary neuropil is characterized by the so-called glomeruli, which comprise a core of dendritic spines that are coupled by dendrodendritic gap junctions and surrounded by axon terminals (Nĕmecek and Wolff, 1969; Bowman and King, 1973; Sotelo et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nĕmecek and Wolff, 1969; Bowman and King, 1973; and Sotelo et al., 1974.

claim: Each and every spine of the entire dendritic arbor of olivary neurons in the PO and rostral MAO is innervated by both an inhibitory and excitatory input.
source: Ultrastructural 3D analysis of olivary neurons in the PO and rostral MAO following the use of a combination of intracellular labeling with double or triple labeling of afferents indicates that each and every spine of the entire dendritic arbor is innervated by both an inhibitory and excitatory input (de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; De Zeeuw, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; and De Zeeuw, 1990.

claim: The vast majority of both inhibitory and excitatory afferents terminate onto dendritic spines within the glomeruli.
source: Moreover, the vast majority of both the inhibitory and excitatory afferents terminates onto these spines within the glomeruli.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the cited studies.

claim: There are only very few local interneurons in the IO.
source: Given that there are only very few local interneurons in the IO (De Zeeuw, 1990; Fredette et al., 1992), this dominant configuration implies that the interaction between the inhibitory and excitatory inputs onto the electronically coupled spines over time is likely to play an important role in IO function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Zeeuw, 1990 and Fredette et al., 1992.

claim: The impact of CN input on STOs differs substantially from that of MDJ input.
source: The impact of CN input on STOs differs substantially from that of MDJ input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing CN and MDJ effects shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: STOs induced by CN input have on average a smaller Vhyp, possibly due to the flooring effect of HCN channels.
source: STOs induced by CN input have on average a smaller Vhyp, possibly due to the flooring effect of HCN channels, while STOs induced by MDJ input show a more depolarized resting membrane potential.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference about HCN channel properties.

claim: STOs induced by CN input slightly, but significantly, outlast those induced by MDJ input.
source: Despite these differences, the STOs induced by CN input slightly, but significantly, outlast those induced by MDJ input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing durations of CN-induced and MDJ-induced oscillations.

claim: The relatively mild phase resetting of MDJ excitation-driven synaptic responses may be related to the conductances recruited during their hyperpolarizing phase.
source: The relatively mild phase resetting and amplitude boost of the MDJ excitation-driven synaptic responses may be related to the conductances that are recruited during their hyperpolarizing phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and knowledge of ion channel properties.

claim: SK and HCN channels mediating the hyperpolarizing component of MDJ responses might be partially inactivated in oscillating neurons during their relatively large membrane depolarizations.
source: These channels might be partially inactivated in oscillating neurons during their relatively large membrane depolarizations (Milligan et al., 2006), reducing the impact of the excitation-mediated Vhyp.
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to Milligan et al., 2006 and experimental observations.

claim: Repetitive release of GABA from cerebellar terminals can reduce the level of coupling in olivary glomeruli.
source: For example, repetitive release of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA from the cerebellar terminals at the olivary spines can reduce the level of coupling (Lang et al., 1996), possibly by shunting the spines with their relatively long necks from the dendrites (Llinas et al., 1974; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; De Zeeuw, 1990), and thereby transiently reduce the strength of the STOs both in vitro (Lefler et al., 2014) and in vivo (Lang, 2002; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012a; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lang et al., 1996; Lefler et al., 2014; Lang, 2002; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012a; and Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012b.

claim: Enduring entrapment of GABA in the glomeruli for about 60 ms may contribute to long-lasting GABAergic effects.
source: Moreover, given the prominent glial sheaths surrounding the core of innervated and coupled dendrites inside the glomeruli (De Zeeuw et al., 1990; De Zeeuw, 1990) and given the observed long-lasting GABAergic effects on the hyperpolarization of IO neurons in both the experimental and modeling data, enduring entrapment of GABA in the glomeruli for about 60 ms may also contribute.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge from citations and experimental observations.

claim: The local impact of excitatory glutamatergic afferents on the level of dendrodendritic coupling in the glomeruli varies depending on the duration and frequency of stimulation.
source: Likewise, depending on the duration and frequency of stimulation, the local impact of the excitatory glutamatergic afferents on the level of dendrodendritic coupling in the glomeruli varies (Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014), which in turn will affect the presence and strength of the STOs (De Gruijl et al., 2014b; Negrello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014; De Gruijl et al., 2014b; and Negrello et al., 2019.

claim: When excitation follows inhibition by 50 ms, the STO amplitude boost is small, likely due to depolarization-driven deactivation of HCN channels.
source: We show that when excitation follows inhibition by 50 ms and hits the peak of the hyperpolarizing component of the CN synaptic response, the STO amplitude boost is small, likely as a result of the depolarization-driven deactivation of HCN channels (Bal and McCormick, 1997; Milligan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference supported by citations to Bal and McCormick, 1997 and Milligan et al., 2006.

claim: The most obvious explanation for reduced spike probability at the 50 ms interval is that excitatory synaptic responses are furthest away from spike threshold.
source: The most obvious explanation for the reduced spike probability at this interval is that excitatory synaptic responses are time-wise furthest away from spike threshold given that excitation arrives at the trough of the hyperpolarizing component of the inhibitory response.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Excitation that follows inhibition by 150 ms is most conducive to spike generation because excitation is presented around the peak of the rebound component of the inhibitory response.
source: Conversely, excitation that follows inhibition by 150 ms is most conducive to spike generation, as excitation is presented around the peak of the rebound component of the inhibitory response, which further brings the cell to spike threshold.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The IO circuitry may allow for phase-based computing that is under control of synaptic inputs from the CN and MDJ.
source: Given that these features were also replicated in our network model and that the size of olivary clusters with sub-cycle phase differences could also be controlled by the inhibitory and excitatory inputs in this model, it is attractive to hypothesize that the IO circuitry may allow for phase-based computing that is under control of the synaptic inputs from the CN and MDJ.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental and modeling data.

claim: Such analog computing system can facilitate the generation of a complex array of properly sequenced actions.
source: Such analog computing system can facilitate the generation of a complex array of properly sequenced actions (Holden et al., 2017), in which the sequence of events can be maintained at a variety of speeds or frequencies (Jacobson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Holden et al., 2017 and Jacobson et al., 2009.

claim: Different IO clusters may be able to generate olivary oscillations with subtle phase differences, supporting intervals shorter than the cycle period.
source: Indeed, in line with the findings from our olivary network model, systems recordings of complex spike activity in the cerebellar cortex using chronically implanted multi-electrode arrays in freely moving rats indicate that the different IO clusters may be able to generate olivary oscillations with subtle phase differences, supporting intervals shorter than the cycle period, and to maintain these oscillations at a constant phase difference across large global changes in frequency (Jacobson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jacobson et al., 2009 and is consistent with modeling results.

claim: Patterns of complex spike activity can be related to ongoing reflex-like behavior and associative sensorimotor behavior.
source: Accordingly, the patterns of complex spike activity can be related to ongoing reflex-like behavior and associative sensorimotor behavior (Welsh et al., 1995; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Welsh et al., 1995; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; and Hoogland et al., 2015.

claim: Disturbing complex spike patterns at the sub-cycle range can affect the latencies of motor behaviors.
source: and disturbing these patterns at the sub-cycle range can affect the latencies of these motor behaviors (Kistler et al., 2002; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kistler et al., 2002 and Van Der Giessen et al., 2008.

claim: The IO may enable the olivo-cerebellar system to gate temporal patterns at different rates without distortion, facilitating execution of the same behavioral task at different speeds.
source: The IO may thus underlie not only rhythmic activity and synchronization, but also temporal patterning that requires CN-MDJ intervals at various cycle durations and that may enable the olivo-cerebellar system to gate temporal patterns at different rates without distortion, facilitating execution of the same behavioral task at different speeds (Welsh et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015; Lawrenson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Welsh et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015; and Lawrenson et al., 2016.

claim: Increases and decreases of complex spike activity are critical for cerebellar motor learning by facilitating induction of long-term depression and potentiation at parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses.
source: In addition to online control of temporal patterns of complex spike activity that may facilitate ongoing coordination of sensorimotor behavior and/or cognitive functions (Welsh et al., 1995; Hoogland et al., 2015; Romano et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2022), increases and decreases of complex spike activity are also critical for cerebellar motor learning in that they facilitate induction of long-term depression and potentiation at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses, respectively (Ito and Kano, 1982; Schonewille et al., 2010; Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ito and Kano, 1982; Schonewille et al., 2010; and Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017.

claim: Long-term depression and long-term potentiation at Purkinje cell synapses are the dominant forms of plasticity in downbound and upbound microzone modules.
source: Long-term depression and long-term potentiation at the Purkinje cell synapses have been proposed to be the dominant forms of plasticity in the so-called downbound and upbound microzones modules (De Zeeuw, 2021; Voerman et al., 2022), which underlie different forms of motor learning dependent on whether they require decreases and increases in simple spike activity, respectively (Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Bina et al., 2022; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Herzfeld et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Zeeuw, 2021; Voerman et al., 2022; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Bina et al., 2022; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; and Herzfeld et al., 2018.

claim: The precise interval between inhibition and excitation of IO neurons determines whether and when complex spike firing frequency will go up or down.
source: Thus, the current finding that the precise interval between inhibition and excitation of IO neurons determines whether and when the complex spike firing frequency will go up or down is probably critical not only for online motor performance, but also for more long-term processes such as motor learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.
